general.temas: The summit between Xi, Trump and Putin in Shenzhen appears in all five newspapers, with attention on its meagre results and the war in Ukraine. Volkswagen’s labour demands, Anthropic’s stock market listing, the controversy over Claudia Roth and the launch of GTA 6 also recur. Among the topics appearing on just one front page, la taz covers the new definition of obesity.
general.motivo_crispacion: Tensions are considerable because of Putin’s threats to Ukraine after the summit and European disagreements over funding for Kyiv. In Germany, prominent issues include criticism of Volkswagen’s wage demands, the debate over the FDP’s relationship with the AfD, and the controversy between Claudia Roth and the Central Council of Jews. An attempted deportation from church sanctuary and allegations of racism in Bremen are also causing friction. These stories are partly offset by reports on sport, video games, health and culture.

Süddeutsche Zeitung.resumen:
- Kompany returns to the Bayern dugout, while Musiala is expected to return.
- An article criticises the taxation of large donations in the wake of the Döpfner case.
- The summit between Xi, Trump and Putin in Shenzhen yields images but few concrete results.
- El Salvador sends troops to Haiti; in Germany, Thomas Bach’s role in the Olympic bid is under scrutiny.
- The front page also covers the memorial to victims of the SED, Anthropic’s stock market listing and video games as art.
Süddeutsche Zeitung.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “Germany’s most unjust tax law” and “a scandal” intensify the criticism, although an explicit opposition between the people and the elites does not predominate.
Süddeutsche Zeitung.sesgo: There is a critical approach to decisions by leaders and influential figures, particularly on tax and sport. Some cultural and opinion pieces make explicit value judgments.

Die Welt.resumen:
- Merz seeks to secure aid for Ukraine through a new credit mechanism amid European divisions.
- VW proposes freezing wages and changing the 35-hour working week to save on personnel costs.
- The front page covers debates about the CDU, the FDP, the AfD and education, as well as the exchange between Josef Schuster and Claudia Roth.
- Prominent stories include an attempted deportation from church sanctuary, security at Magdeburg’s Christmas market and the ban on full-face veils in schools in North Rhine-Westphalia.
- In international news, the Trump-Putin-Xi summit is analysed; a price cut on Apple headphones is also announced.
Die Welt.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “risky gamble”, “chaos” and “survival guide” intensify the conflict, although an explicit opposition between the people and the elites does not predominate.
Die Welt.sesgo: The selection emphasises political confrontation, security and disagreements, with several headlines focusing on controversies and risks. The available information does not reveal an unambiguous ideological orientation.

Der Spiegel.resumen:
- Mercedes faces the risk of a sales ban in the US; Volkswagen calls for cuts and changes to working hours.
- The meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi ended without substantial agreements, while Berlin hosts contacts to explore peace talks on Ukraine.
- The International Court of Justice finds that Myanmar’s military committed genocide against the Rohingya.
- An anonymous survey raises criticisms of Minister Ina Scharrenbach; Claudia Roth’s statements on Israel spark controversy among the Greens.
- Other stories cover energy consumption for cooling, Anthropic’s stock market listing, Deutsche Bank, employee compensation and BASF’s failed purchase of Evonik.
Der Spiegel.motivo_populismo: Reporting predominates, although expressions such as “more work for less money”, “bad boss” and “risky gamble” emphasise conflict or risk.
Der Spiegel.sesgo: The selection pays particular attention to German industry and to labour, business and political conflicts, taking a critical approach to some decisions and figures. No clear partisan orientation is apparent from these headlines.

Bild.resumen:
- The front page highlights the summit between Xi, Putin and Trump, with headlines about the treatment of Putin and the peace declaration.
- Vanessa Bryant plans to enter the basketball business; a poker scandal in California is also covered.
- Sports news includes a Mainz player’s contract renewal, an injury to a Nuremberg defender and a profile of Brajan Gruda.
- GTA 6 players report technical glitches and some are asking for their money back.
- The investigation into a double murder from 55 years ago is reopened, and the possible danger of living alongside bears in Germany is raised.
Bild.motivo_populismo: The tone relies on sensationalism and emotional language, with expressions such as “Xi humiliates Putin”, “poker scandal” and “players are climbing the walls”, although there are hardly any appeals to the people against the elites.
Bild.sesgo: The selection favours entertainment, sport and personal conflicts, with wording that emphasises confrontation, danger and surprise. No defined political orientation is apparent in the headlines provided.

taz.resumen:
- A new definition of obesity expands diagnosis beyond the body mass index.
- The expansion of temporary employment rules is presented as detrimental to young people.
- The German foreign minister’s visit to Azerbaijan raises questions about interests and values.
- A Van Gogh work fetches $190.4 million at auction, following a dispute over its history during the Nazi era.
- Other topics include local consent for AI data centres, racism in Bremen’s fire service and the meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi.
taz.motivo_populismo: An informative tone predominates, although expressions such as “new cause for anger” and “a slap in the face” heighten the emotional impact of the story about employment contracts.
taz.sesgo: The front page pays attention to protecting young workers, the consent of local communities and exposing racism. It also takes a critical approach to German diplomacy in Azerbaijan.

opiniones.comunista:
Today I see the class struggle in two headlines: Volkswagen proposes freezing wages and challenging the 35-hour week, while a large transfer of wealth by gift was reportedly barely taxed at all, according to investigations cited in the press. Working people are being asked to accept more effort and fewer rights; the system allows the very wealthy to retain their privileges.

I do not believe competitiveness justifies placing the burden of the crisis on the workforce. I support collective bargaining and union organising, but also a deeper transformation: collective ownership of strategic sectors and economic decisions subject to democratic control by those who produce and by society. Fair taxation of great fortunes should sustain universal public services. Wealth is the product of collective labour; its benefits should not be concentrated in a few hands.
opiniones.anarquista:
I see the same distribution of power in very different stories. Volkswagen is calling for a wage freeze and cuts to the 35-hour working week: working people must bear the cost of decisions they do not control. I do not expect a political party to hand them justice; I have more faith in their independent organisation, their solidarity and their ability to decide collectively how and for whom to produce.

In Bremerhaven, police forced open the door of a church during a failed deportation attempt. In the face of that authority, the refuge offered by a community expresses a different idea of responsibility: caring for a person without reducing them to a case file.

The expansion of data centres, too, should depend on the consent of those who live nearby, not just investors or governments. For me, freedom does not mean choosing between obeying the state and obeying the market, but building alternatives together without masters.
opiniones.liberal:
Shenzhen’s transformation reminds me why I support economic openness: when people can trade, invest and start businesses, they create opportunities that no state plan can devise from behind a desk. Photos of the summit, without concrete agreements, are worth far less than stable rules and free exchange.

I also believe the German debate on inheritances and gifts points to a real problem: a system that grants major advantages to those who can exploit its loopholes erodes equality before the law. My response is not to raise taxes indiscriminately, but to establish low rates and simple rules and eliminate privileges. And when it comes to Volkswagen’s wage demands, I prefer free and responsible negotiations between the company and its workers to solutions dictated by the government. Competitiveness matters, but so does employees’ right to defend their working conditions.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
I worry that Germany is learning to live with what it should be fighting. Magdeburg’s Christmas market will open protected by hundreds of bollards: I appreciate the precaution, but a tradition should not need a fortress to survive. Security requires prevention and a state capable of enforcing its laws.

That is why I support strict immigration controls and the enforcement of legally authorised deportations, with judicial safeguards. Church sanctuary deserves respect, but it cannot become a permanent exception to the law.

I also distrust a political class that seeks to commit long-term funding to Ukraine while Volkswagen proposes wage freezes and cuts for its workers. I do not deny the importance of Ukraine, but I demand that Germany preserve its ability to make its own decisions and put the security and prosperity of its own people first.
opiniones.centro:
Images of the Shenzhen summit are no substitute for concrete agreements. I am particularly concerned that peace in Ukraine should be discussed without Europe being relegated to listening to decisions made by others. Sustained support for Ukraine requires credible funding, but also deliberation and consensus within the European Union. Diplomacy is indispensable; it must not be confused with accepting just any agreement.

At home, Volkswagen’s demands reveal another tension: a company needs competitiveness, but asking for more work and freezing wages cannot be the only response to a crisis. I have more faith in collective bargaining than in imposing the cost of adjustment on workers. And if we want to sustain an open economy, we must also correct tax privileges on inheritances and gifts: fair rules strengthen both confidence in the market and social protection.
